adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The harbour town woke slowly. Fishing boats nudged against the quay while gulls quarrelled over scraps, and the bakery lights came on before the sky had settled on a colour. Marta had run the chandlery for thirty-one years, and she still opened the shutters herself, one at a time, in the same order her father had used.

Deliveries came by van from the mainland twice a week: rope, paint, lamp oil, brass fittings, and a crate of charts that nobody had ordered and nobody would claim. Marta signed for the crate, stacked it behind the counter, and forgot about it until Thursday, when a young woman in a raincoat asked whether anything had arrived addressed to a boat named Selkie.

Third shelf, Marta said, behind the tide tables.

The woman found the crate and carried it to the window seat, where the light was best. Inside were charts of a coastline Marta did not recognise: a long shallow bay, three islands shaped like sleeping animals, soundings marked in a hand so careful it might have been printed. At the bottom lay a logbook with a cracked spine and a name inked inside the cover.

They read it together over tea. The entries were ordinary at first, lists of wind and weather, hours lost to fog, a pump repaired with wire and stubbornness. Then, in the middle of a page, the handwriting changed. The wind had turned, the entry said, and the writer had decided to run for the islands rather than beat back to the harbour. Nobody in the town had ever heard of a boat making that passage in a single night.

Marta turned the page and found a sketch of the bay, with a small cross marking a cove she had never seen noted on any chart. The woman said her grandfather had kept a boat called Selkie and had drowned in the year the logbook stopped. She had grown up on stories of him and had come to the coast to learn whether any of them were true.

The afternoon passed. The shop bell rang twice; a man bought rope, and a boy counted his coins twice before buying a bag of galvanised nails. Outside, the tide crept over the mudflats, and the light went from white to a softer, heavier grey. Marta brought out the old brass lamp and lit it, and the two of them sat with the charts spread between the teacups, tracing a route through water too shallow for any sensible skipper.

By evening they had decided nothing except that the story deserved telling. The woman rolled the charts carefully, thanked Marta twice, and walked out into the drizzle with the crate under her arm. Marta stood in the doorway and watched the rain stitch the harbour to the sky.

Back inside, she wiped the counter, banked the stove, and hung the copper pan on its hook for the morning.
